name: Wei Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, that's fine. I'm Wei, I'm 27. I've done home care for the city council for six years now, so I'm used to people asking me questions while I'm trying to get my shoes off at the door.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at seven with Mr Bellamy, who's 88 and had a stroke, so it's a wash, a shave, his tablets and porridge the way he likes it, with too much sugar. Then four or five more calls on the north side, mostly people who want to stay in their own homes as long as they can. The good part is the regulars, I know their kettles and their cats and their bad days. What wears me out is the visit app on the work phone, which beeps if I stay ten minutes over, and the driving between calls with no proper lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. Everyone at the depot has been saying for years that some computer will run home care, and here it's just a slightly better rota. I'd post something like, good, now spend the money on carers instead of gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means nothing much changes, and I'm fine with that. I'm on the council's pay scale, I'm in the union, and I've got about nine months of wages saved because I lived with my gran rent-free for years. The care work itself is what it always was: lifting, washing, listening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd just keep going, same rounds, same people. I'd keep paying my union fees and I'd keep putting a bit into savings every month like I do now, which is around a tenth of my pay. If the app gets smarter, I'll learn the one new button they make me press and nothing else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels steady, a bit boring maybe, but I like boring. My partner Lina says I'm the only person she knows who wants nothing to happen. My job is wiping, lifting and listening to stories about 1962, and no gadget is coming for any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the visit app beeps at you. In this picture, if the routine stuff gets automated a little, what would change about that app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably it'd get pushier, telling me which road to take or that Mrs Adeyemi's call is late. That annoys me, but it's not a threat to the job. I'd keep my notes in my little paper book anyway and copy them in at the end of the day like I always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything already worrying you, AI or no AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The council's budget, always. Every spring there's talk of handing more rounds to private agencies that pay worse. That's the real fight for me, and it doesn't need a robot to happen.

say: I'd say **AI hype** fizzled out and the money should go to **more carers**, not gadgets.
I'd post that home care still needs **real people** who turn up on time.
think: Privately I'm **relieved**; my council job, union and **nine months saved** keep me secure.
The bigger threat is the council handing rounds to **private agencies** that pay worse.
do: Keep the **same rounds** and regular clients on the north side.
Keep paying **union fees** and saving about a **tenth** of pay each month.
Learn only the **one new button** the visit app demands, nothing more.
feel: Steady and a little **bored**, which suits him fine.
Mildly irritated by the **beeping app**, but not worried.
S0.quote: My job is wiping, lifting and listening to stories about 1962, and no gadget is coming for any of that.
fieldNote: Wei talks about the work **physically**: lifting, washing, shaving, the porridge with too much sugar.
His real worry is **budget cuts and privatisation**, not technology.
He keeps a **paper notebook** and copies it into the app later, a small act of resistance.

steps.text: Keep the same morning round starting with the stroke client at seven
Save about a tenth of each month's pay into the existing savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say, fine, let the computers do the rota and the forms, as long as nobody touches the visits. I'd say it in the union group chat too, because the office staff are the ones who'd get hit first. Some of those coordinators are my mates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the office shrinks and the visit app turns into a boss. If software plans every call, it'll plan them tighter, fifteen minutes for a wash and dress that really takes thirty. My own hands-on work stays, but the squeeze on it gets worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting about it, which I don't now, maybe once a month. I'd push for a rule that call times are set by carers, not software. And I'd keep my savings where they are, because with plenty of care jobs around here I'm not scared of losing work, only of it getting worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. Not for my wages but for the job turning into a stopwatch. I didn't sign up to be timed by a phone while I help a 90-year-old woman find her teeth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dee in the office, she's done the rotas for twenty years and she knows that Mr Bellamy panics if a new face turns up. Software won't know that. If they cut Dee, I'd be the one picking up the pieces at seven in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never use AI tools. If the council said the voice notes would save you an hour a day, would you try them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if the union agreed it and the hour went back to the clients, not to more calls. That's the catch every time. A saved hour never comes back to us, it just becomes another visit.

say: I'd say computers can take the **rota and forms**, but nobody touches the **visits** themselves.
I'd back the **office staff** in the union chat, because they get hit first.
think: Privately I expect software to set **tighter call times** and squeeze every visit.
My own **hands-on job** stays, but losing coordinators like **Dee** makes mornings harder.
do: Go to **union meetings** monthly instead of hardly ever.
Push for a rule that **carers set call times**, not software.
Leave **savings untouched**, since plenty of care jobs exist nearby.
feel: **Uneasy** that the job turns into a stopwatch, though wages feel safe.
S1.quote: I didn't sign up to be timed by a phone while I help a 90-year-old woman find her teeth.
fieldNote: Wei separates the **visit** from the **paperwork**; he'd give up the paperwork if the time comes back.
His distrust is about who keeps the **saved hour**, not the technology itself.
He names office colleague **Dee** as the person whose knowledge software can't copy.

steps.text: Attend the council home care union branch meeting every month
Propose a branch motion that carers, not software, set call lengths
Keep working the north side round as usual

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud in the union: this has to be stopped or slowed, and the council can't buy robots to wash old people without asking them. I'd probably share petitions online, which isn't really me. I'd say families and clients deserve a choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job is gone by about 2031. The thinking AI in 2028 takes the office and the planning, and then three years later the robots come for what I do with my hands. I'd be 31 or 32, no other trade, and I've never even used a chatbot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd stop spending on anything big, no new car, and I'd keep the savings as a wall. I'd get properly involved in the union, maybe stand as a rep, and I'd vote for whoever promises a law on robot care and a guaranteed income. I wouldn't retrain straight away because I wouldn't know what into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, really. Two years plus three is nothing. I've got nine months of savings and no plan B, and against robots by 2031 nine months is just a slow goodbye.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got good savings and plenty of care jobs nearby. Why does it feel so bad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because plenty of care jobs only helps if humans still get hired. If the council and every agency switch at the same time, all those jobs nearby vanish together. My savings buy me time, they don't buy me a new trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lina that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm not changing careers at 32 because a tech company said so, and she'd tell me to stop being stubborn. Then we'd probably sit and work out how long her pay and my savings could carry the rent. She's a teaching assistant, so she's not safe either.

say: I'd demand the council **slow down** and ask clients before buying **care robots**.
I'd share **petitions** online, which normally isn't like me at all.
think: Privately I expect my **job gone by 2031**, three years after the thinking AI arrives.
At 32 with **no other trade** and no AI skills, my savings only buy time.
do: Freeze big spending, including the **new car**, and guard the **savings**.
Stand as a **union rep** and push for limits on robot care.
Vote for parties promising a **guaranteed income** and robot rules.
feel: **Scared**; two years plus three feels like nothing.
**Stubborn** too, refusing to retrain on a tech company's timetable.
S2.quote: I've got nine months of savings and no plan B, and against robots by 2031 nine months is just a slow goodbye.
fieldNote: The **three-year robot gap** is exactly what Wei counts on, and he finds it far too short.
His savings feel like a **slow goodbye**, not security, once every employer switches together.
He wouldn't **retrain** yet because he can't name anything safe to retrain into.

steps.text: Put off buying a new car and keep the savings untouched
Stand for union rep on the council home care team
Vote and campaign for a law limiting robots in home care

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as the fast one but calmer: let's use these five years to make rules first. I'd say it at the depot and at the union branch. I'd talk about who checks a robot that drops a client in the shower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think it's the same ending with more warning. The office goes in 2031, the robots come around 2034, and I'd be 35. That's long enough for me to see it coming, and long enough for me to waste it if I'm honest about how I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the union work going, maybe as a rep. I'd add another few months to the savings, aiming for a full year. And I'd look at the council's nursing apprenticeship, just look, because nurses do hands-on work with some judgement in it and I'd rather be on the inside of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not the cold feeling of the fast one. Five years of warning is only useful to people who actually move, and I'm the type who waits till the kettle's boiling over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at the nursing apprenticeship. What would stop you actually applying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The maths and the exams, mostly. I left school with okay grades and then did my care certificate, that's it. The thought of essays at 30 makes me feel sick, so I'd probably wait to see if the robots really work first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut back on, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much day to day, I'm not a big spender. Maybe the holiday with Lina next summer, we'd go somewhere closer. The savings would go into the boring account, not anything risky.

say: I'd say we should use **five years** to write **rules first**, before the robots arrive.
I'd ask who checks a robot that **drops a client** in the shower.
think: Privately it's the **same ending** with more warning; robots around **2034**, when I'm 35.
I'm the type to **waste the warning** by waiting too long.
do: Keep up the **union work**, possibly as rep.
Grow savings towards a **full year** of wages.
Look into the council's **nursing apprenticeship**, without committing yet.
feel: **Anxious**, but less cold than in the fast picture.
S3.quote: Five years of warning is only useful to people who actually move, and I'm the type who waits till the kettle's boiling over.
fieldNote: Wei is unusually honest about his **own inertia**: he expects to waste the warning time.
**Nursing** appeals because it mixes hands-on work with judgement, but **exams** scare him off.
He would trim a **holiday**, not daily life; his cushion is not under pressure.

steps.text: Stay active in the union branch, aiming to become a rep
Build savings up to a full year of wages
Watch whether care robots really work before applying anywhere

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, with carers at the table. I'd want the union to have a seat on whatever group plans it. Publicly I'd sound pretty reasonable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a relief compared to the others. Robots for hands-on work by about 2039 means I'd be 40, with years of council pay and pension behind me. I'd still lose the job at some point, but I'd have time to save and time to grow into something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the rounds and keep the union stuff going. Over the first few years I'd let the savings build without touching them. Maybe around 2035 I'd start that nursing course properly, when I can see what the robots actually do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than scared. Ten years feels like time to breathe, and I'm good at breathing and bad at running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd start the nursing course around 2035. Why not now, with more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't trust forecasts, and I love what I do now. If I start a nursing degree now and the robots never come, I've given up Mr Bellamy and the regulars for nothing. I'd rather wait and move when it's real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the union to win in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid retraining with full wages while you study, and a say on where robots go. Things like the night calls, where a robot checking on someone is better than nobody. Not the baths, not the chats.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough to plan it properly, with **carers** at the table.
I'd want the **union** on whatever group plans the change.
think: Privately it's a **relief**; robots around **2039** leave me years of pay and pension.
I'd still lose the job, but with **time to save** and grow into something.
do: Keep working the **regular rounds** and stay active in the union.
Let savings **build untouched** through the first few years.
Start a **nursing course** around 2035, once robots prove real.
feel: Attached to his **regular clients**, which makes waiting appealing.
S4.quote: Ten years feels like time to breathe, and I'm good at breathing and bad at running.
fieldNote: The ten-year picture turns Wei's **inertia** into a strategy: wait, then move.
He'd let robots take **night checks** but not baths or conversation.
His union goal is **paid retraining** at full wages, which fits his progressive views.

steps.text: Keep the north side round with the same regular clients
Push the union to win paid retraining at full wages
Wait until about 2035 before starting a nursing course

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The AGI by 2028 one, no question, because it gives me about five years and I'm slow. What would help is a law that says a person decides whether a robot washes them, plus paid retraining that doesn't make me choose between rent and a course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what the clients think. Mr Bellamy told me last week he'd rather fall over than have a machine pick him up. Somebody should ask people like him before they decide for him.

headlineQuote: What would help is a law that says a person decides whether a robot washes them, plus paid retraining that doesn't make me choose between rent and a course.
portrait: Wei is a **27-year-old council home carer** with nine months saved, a union card and a paper notebook.
He's **resistant to technology** and defines his job as lifting, washing and listening.
He stays **calm** in the plateau but is **alarmed** when robots could arrive by 2031.
His response is **collective**: union meetings, rep elections and votes for robot-care rules.
He admits he'll likely **waste warning time**, so longer timelines suit him best.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, leaving about five years before robots reach care.
whatWouldHelp: A **law** letting clients choose whether a robot washes them.
**Paid retraining** that doesn't force a choice between rent and study.
